paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Anyone who has travelled widely knows that people in different regions speak the same language with different accents. It may be surprising to learn that many birds do the same. Songbirds of a single species often sing noticeably different versions of their song depending on where they live, and researchers who record them can sometimes tell which valley or town a bird comes from simply by listening. The differences may be small to the human ear, such as an extra note or a slightly longer pause, but they are consistent enough to be measured by computer.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: These regional differences exist because songbirds, unlike most other animals, learn their songs. A young male listens to the adult birds around him during his first few months of life and gradually practises until his own song matches theirs. If a chick is raised in isolation and never hears an adult, it produces only a simple, poorly formed song. Small copying errors, passed from one generation to the next, slowly create local dialects, in much the same way that human accents develop.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dialects can change surprisingly quickly. In one long-term study of sparrows in North America, a new ending to the species' song first appeared in a small western population. Within about twenty years it had spread across thousands of kilometres, replacing the older version almost completely. Researchers believe that young birds spending the winter in mixed flocks picked up the new ending and carried it home in spring.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Dialects may matter for breeding. In several species, females respond more strongly to males that sing the local version of the song, perhaps because it suggests that a male is well adapted to local conditions. A male that arrives from far away with an unfamiliar song may therefore find it harder to attract a mate. For conservation workers who move birds to new areas to protect them, this can be an unexpected problem, since the relocated birds may struggle to breed with the local population.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Human activity is now affecting bird song too. In noisy cities, some birds sing at a higher pitch than their relatives in the countryside, which helps their songs to be heard above the low rumble of traffic. Scientists are still debating whether these changes are learnt or inherited, but they show that bird song, like human speech, is constantly shaped by the environment in which it is used.
